solution.description: Both 7 and 8 sit just below 10, so 10 is the working base for this Nikhilam multiplication.
Record how far each number falls short of the base: 7 is 3 below 10 and 8 is 2 below, so the deviations are minus 3 and minus 2.
Cross-subtract to get the left part: add one number to the other's deviation, 7 plus minus 2, or 8 plus minus 3. Both routes land on 5.
Multiply the two deviations, minus 3 by minus 2. Two negatives give a positive, so the right part is 6.
Put the parts together: multiply the left part 5 by the base 10 and add the right part 6, which reads off as 56.
Check the shortcut against ordinary multiplication: 7 times 8 really is 56, so the base method has not drifted.
Both 95 and 92 lie just under 100, so 100 is the nearest power of ten to work from and becomes the base for this example.
Write each number with its deficit from the base: 95 is 5 short of 100 and 92 is 8 short, giving deviations of minus 5 and minus 8.
Build the left part by adding the two numbers and taking off one base: 95 plus 92 is 187, minus 100 leaves 87.
The same left part comes from cross-subtraction: take the 8 off 95, or the 5 off 92. Either route gives 87, so use whichever is easier mentally.
Multiply the two deficits, minus 5 by minus 8, for a right part of positive 40.
Base 100 allows two digits on the right, and 40 already fills both, so write the left part 87 followed by 40 to read 8740.

solution.description: Choose 100 as the base: it is the nearest power of ten to both 75 and 92, which is the setup the Nikhilam sutra needs.
Write each number against that base: 75 is 25 below 100 and 92 is 8 below, so the deviations are minus 25 and minus 8.
State the pattern this example will follow: the left part is one number reduced by the other's deviation and then scaled by 100, and the right part is the product of the two deviations.
Compute the left part by cross-subtraction: 75 minus 8, or equivalently 92 minus 25. Both give 67.
Multiply the deviations, minus 25 by minus 8. Both are negative, so the right part is a positive 200.
Scale the left part by the base, 67 times 100 is 6700, then add the right part: 6700 plus 200 is 6900. The right part runs to three digits, so it is added in rather than written alongside.

key_reminders: {'point': 'But now we have 3 digits instead of 2 in the right hand part: we will have to carry over.'}
{'point': "We don't need to do this when there is no carry over, but we would get the same answer."}
{'point': 'You can see how to extend this easily to base 1000, 10000, etc.'}
{'point': 'All the examples so far have shown numbers less than the base.'}
{'point': 'What happens if we are multiplying numbers just above 10, 100 etc.?'}
common_mistakes: Writing 67 and 200 side by side to read 67200 or 6720. Base 100 leaves only two digits on the right, so the extra hundred has to carry into the left part.
Cross-subtracting the wrong pair, such as 75 minus 25 or 92 minus 8, instead of taking each number's partner deviation.
Making the right part negative. Minus 25 times minus 8 is a positive 200.
repair_note: Descriptions were generic or restated the formula rather than the step; all six rewritten against their own operation and result for 75 x 92 at base 100. technique_name (base multiplication) and visual_scaffold (arrow_matrix) already matched the cross-subtraction work. Added three common_mistakes because the right part 200 overflows the two digits base 100 allows, a real hazard with these numbers.

solution.description: The numbers 14 and 18 are both close to 10, which is a power of 10, making it suitable for the Nikhilam method.
Calculate how much each number differs from the base. Both are above the base, so deviations are positive.

solution.operation: Calculate left side (sum of number and other's deviation)
solution.description: Add either number to the other's deviation from the base. Both ways give the same result.
Multiply the deviations from the base. Since both deviations are positive, their product is positive.
The left side is multiplied by the base (10) and added to the right side to get the final product.
The same two numbers as before, with the order swapped. Measure each against base 10: 18 is 8 above and 14 is 4 above, so both deviations are positive.
Add one number to the other's deviation to get the left part: 18 plus 4 gives 22, exactly the 22 that 14 plus 8 produced in the first example.
Multiply the two deviations, 8 times 4, giving 32 as the right part.
Combine the two parts: 22 times the base 10 is 220, and adding 32 gives 252. The answer matches the first example, so the order of the two numbers makes no difference.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Note that the right side should only have 1 place for base 10, so there is a carry over.'}
{'point': 'If you have trouble with this, always multiply the left part by the base and add the right hand part, and you will be safe.'}
{'point': 'You may wonder if you need to do this in a particular order.'}
{'point': 'The answer is no, as you will see when we repeat this example with the numbers swapped.'}
common_mistakes: Reading the answer straight off as 2232 by placing 32 beside 22. Base 10 leaves only one digit on the right, so the 3 must carry into the left part.
Subtracting the deviations from the base out of habit. Both 14 and 18 are above 10, so the deviations are plus 4 and plus 8 and they are added.
repair_note: Example 2 (18 x 14) had vague placeholder descriptions on steps with empty results; each was rewritten to name the actual deviations and partial results for these numbers, while example 1 descriptions were already correct for their steps and were left as written. Scaffold and technique_name unchanged and correct. Added two common_mistakes: the right part 32 exceeds the single digit base 10 allows, and above-base deviations are commonly subtracted by mistake.

solution.description: Both 104 and 98 sit within a few units of 100, so 100 is the base for this working.
Write each number as the base plus or minus its deviation: 104 is 4 above 100 and 98 is 2 below, giving plus 4 and minus 2.

solution.operation: Apply Nikhilam formula: (x + a)(x + b) = x(x + a + b) + ab
solution.description: Apply the base identity with x equal to 100, a equal to 4 and b equal to minus 2, which turns the product into a base multiple plus a small correction.

solution.operation: Calculate left part (sum of number and deviation of the other)
solution.description: Add the two deviations to the base to get the left part: 4 plus minus 2 is 2, and 100 plus 2 gives 102.
Multiply the deviations, 4 times minus 2. One is negative, so the right part is minus 8.
Scale the left part by the base, 102 times 100 is 10200, then apply the right part. Because it is negative, subtract: 10200 minus 8 is 10192.
Confirm the shortcut by expanding the brackets term by term, which rebuilds 10192 the long way and shows the base method lost nothing.

solution.operation: Identify base: 1000. Subtract 1000 from both numbers: 1044 → +44, 1002 → +2.
solution.description: Take 1000 as the base, since both numbers sit just above it, and record the surpluses: 1044 is 44 over and 1002 is 2 over.
Find the left part: 1044 plus 1002 minus one base gives 1046, and the quicker routes 1044 plus 2 or 1002 plus 44 give the same 1046.
Multiply the two surpluses, 44 times 2, to get a right part of 88.
Assemble the answer. Base 1000 allows three digits on the right, so 88 is padded to 088 and written after 1046, reading 1046088.
Reach the same figure by expanding instead of appending: 1046 times 1000 is 1046000, and adding 88 gives 1046088.

solution.description: Set out the base identity for this pair, with 1000 as the base and 44 and minus 2 as the deviations, so the product becomes a base multiple plus the product of the deviations.

solution.description: Choose 100 as the base for 63 and 92, and note the identity the method rests on: the base times the base plus both deviations, plus the product of the deviations.
Measure each number against the base: 63 is 37 short of 100 and 92 is 8 short, giving deviations of minus 37 and minus 8.
Get the left part by any of three equivalent routes: 63 plus 92 minus 100, or 63 minus 8, or 92 minus 37. All three give 55.
Multiply the two deviations, minus 37 by minus 8. Both are negative, so the right part is a positive 296.
Combine the parts: 55 times 100 is 5500, and adding 296 gives 5796. The right part runs to three digits, so it is added in rather than appended.

config.description: Straight-division place-value chart for 84 ÷ 7: dividend digits 8|4 in tens and units columns with a quotient digit written under each; the remainder 1 from the tens column is handed into the units column to form gross dividend 14.
config.textual_equivalent: 84 ÷ 7: 8 ÷ 7 = 1 remainder 1; bring down 4 to form gross dividend 14; 14 ÷ 7 = 2 remainder 0; quotient digits 1 and 2 give 12.

examples.problem_statement: Divide 84 by 7 using the Dhvajanka Sutra (Flag Division method).

solution.description: For single-digit divisors, the entire divisor is the main divisor. We set up 7 as the divisor.
Divide the first digit of the dividend (8) by the divisor (7). The quotient is 1 and remainder is 1.
Bring down the next digit (4) and append it to the remainder (1) to form the gross dividend.
Divide the gross dividend (14) by the divisor (7) to get the next quotient digit (2) and remainder (0).
Combine all quotient digits to get 12. Since the remainder is 0, the division is exact.

common_mistakes: Forming the gross dividend as 4 instead of 14 by dropping the remainder 1 from the tens column before bringing the 4 down.
repair_note: Descriptions were already correct for their steps; lightly left as written. Added one common_mistakes entry for the genuine hazard in 84 divided by 7, dropping the tens-column remainder when forming the gross dividend 14. technique_name (division) and place_value_chart scaffold already match the columnar work.

config.description: Divisor 13 split into main 1 | flag 3 lanes over dividend digits 9|1; a diagonal arrow carries the crosswise product 9×3=27 into the adjustment lane, where it is subtracted from gross dividend 91 before the quotient is corrected to 7.
config.textual_equivalent: 91 ÷ 13, main 1 flag 3: tentative 9 ÷ 1 = 9; crosswise product 9×3 = 27; 91 − 27 = 64 shows 9 is too large; corrected quotient 7 since 7×13 = 91.

examples.problem_statement: Divide 91 by 13 using the Dhvajanka Sutra (Flag Division method).

solution.description: Split the divisor 13 into a main part and a flag: the leading 1 is the main divisor and the last digit 3 becomes the flag.

solution.operation: Divide first digit by main divisor
solution.description: Divide the first digit of the dividend, 9, by the main divisor 1 to get a tentative quotient of 9. This is only a first estimate, since the flag has not been paid for yet.
Charge the flag against that estimate: multiply the tentative quotient 9 by the flag digit 3, giving an adjustment of 27.
Rebuild the gross dividend from the digits, 9 tens and 1 unit make 91, then subtract the flag adjustment of 27 to leave 64.

solution.result:
64 ÷ 13 = 4, remainder 12
But 9 is too large, try 7
solution.description: The leftover 64 is far larger than the divisor 13, which shows the tentative 9 was too big. Step the quotient down and test smaller values.
Test 7: 7 times 13 is exactly 91, so the quotient is 7 and nothing is left over.

common_mistakes: Answering 9 because 9 divided by the main digit 1 is 9, without ever subtracting the flag product 9 times 3.
Multiplying the flag digit by the wrong number, for example 13 times 3, instead of by the tentative quotient.
repair_note: Descriptions were rewritten so each names its own operation, in particular the flag adjustment step and the downward re-estimate that the original narrated only loosely. technique_name (division) and arrow_matrix scaffold match the crosswise flag product. Added two common_mistakes about stopping at the tentative quotient 9 and mis-forming the flag product.

config.description: Columnar chart for 72 ÷ 8: dividend digits 7|2 in tens and units columns; leading quotient digit 0 with remainder 7 handed into the units column to form 72, quotient digits 0|9 assembled to 9.
config.textual_equivalent: 72 ÷ 8: 7 ÷ 8 = 0 remainder 7; bring down 2 to form gross dividend 72; 72 ÷ 8 = 9 remainder 0; quotient digits 0 and 9 give 9.

examples.problem_statement: Divide 72 by 8 using the Dhvajanka Sutra (Flag Division method).

solution.description: The divisor 8 is a single digit, so there is no flag to peel off and the whole of 8 acts as the main divisor.
Divide the first digit, 7, by 8. Since 7 is smaller than 8 the quotient digit is 0 and the entire 7 stays behind as remainder.
Hand that remainder into the next column: 7 tens plus the digit 2 rebuilds the gross dividend 72.
Divide the gross dividend 72 by 8 to get the next quotient digit, 9, with nothing left over.
Assemble the quotient digits 0 and 9 into 09, which is simply 9, and the remainder is 0 so the division is exact.

common_mistakes: Forcing a nonzero first quotient digit because 7 will not take an 8, instead of writing 0 and passing the whole 7 into the units column.
